q-136312:
The speed of a particle equals the magnitude of its velocity.

Therefore, the speed of the particle is

$$
\begin{aligned}|u| & =|i+4j| \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+16} \\  & =\sqrt{17} \\  & ≈4.12\,\text{km/h}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

q-136341:
Recall that when a particle moves with constant acceleration, the velocity vector at time $t$ can be found using

$$
v=u+at,
$$

where $u$ is the initial velocity, and $a$ is the acceleration of the particle.

Here, we have

$$
u=-i+4j,\,a=2i+j.
$$

Therefore, after $t=6\,\text{h},$ the velocity of the particle will be

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =u+at \\  & =(-i+4j)+(2i+j)(6) \\  & =(-i+4j)+(12i+6j) \\  & =(11i+10j)\,\text{km/h}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-136289:
Recall that when a particle moves with constant acceleration, the velocity vector at time $t$ can be found using

$$
v=u+at,
$$

where $u$ is the initial velocity, and $a$ is the acceleration of the particle.

Substituting 

$$
u=-2i-8j,\,v=2i,\,t=4,
$$

into the equation above, we can solve for $a,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =u+at \\ 2i & =(-2i-8j)+a(4) \\ 4i+8j & =4a \\ a & =\frac{1}{4}(4i+8j) \\  & =(i+2j)\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-136291:
Recall that when a particle moves with constant acceleration, the velocity vector at time $t$ can be found using

$$
v=u+at,
$$

where $u$ is the initial velocity, and $a$ is the acceleration of the particle.

Substituting 

$$
a=3i+2j,\,u=-7i-6j,\,v=2i
$$

into the equation above, we can solve for $t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =u+at \\ 2i & =(-7i-6j)+(3i+2j)t \\ 9i+6j & =(3i+2j)t \\ 9i+6j & =3ti+2tj\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the $i$ and $j$ components in the last equation, we obtain

$$
{\begin{aligned}9=3t \\ 6=2t\end{aligned}\,⟹\,t=3\,\text{s}.
$$

q-47854:
There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator. So, we find the vertical asymptotes by setting the denominator equal to zero:

$$
x-\sqrt{2}=0\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{2}.
$$

Consequently, $x=\sqrt{2}$ is the only vertical asymptote of $y=f(x),$ as shown below.

q-68167:
Let's simplify the expression by factoring both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x-2{x}^{2}}{18-12x} & =\frac{x(3-2x)}{6(3-2x)}=\frac{x}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the denominator is never zero, we conclude that this function has no vertical asymptotes. A plot of the function is below. Note that it is not defined at $x=\frac{3}{2}.$

q-107068:
Let's simplify the expression by factoring both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x+4)({x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}-5x)}{{x}^{2}+4x} & =\frac{x(x+4)({x}^{2}+3x-5)}{x(x+4)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{x(x+4)}({x}^{2}+3x-5)}{\cancel{x(x+4)}} \\  & ={x}^{2}+3x-5\end{aligned}
$$

Since the denominator is never zero, we conclude that this function has no vertical asymptotes. A plot of the function is below. Note that it is not defined at $x=-4$ and $x=0.$

q-107074:
First, let's put the two terms over a common denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+3}-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}+1} & =\frac{(2{x}^{2}+1)-({x}^{2}+3)}{({x}^{2}+3)(2{x}^{2}+1)}=\frac{{x}^{2}-2}{({x}^{2}+3)(2{x}^{2}+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we proceed to set the denominator equal to zero and get

$$
({x}^{2}+3)(2{x}^{2}+1)=0.
$$

This equation has no real solutions, therefore $f(x)$ has no vertical asymptotes.

q-142026:
Recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

Applying the sum formula for sine with $u=x$ and $v=\frac{7\pi }{6},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+\frac{7\pi }{6}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\frac{-1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-76067:
Our function consists of two radical functions, so it is continuous over all points in its domain.

- To find the domain of $\sqrt{6+x}$, we set the expression under the radical to be greater than or equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}6+x\ge 0\,⟹\,x\ge -6\end{aligned}
$$

- To find the domain of $\sqrt{5x+10}$, we set the expression under the radical to be greater than or equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x+10\ge 0\,⟹\,5x\ge -10\,⟹\,x\ge -2\end{aligned}
$$

The domain of $f(x)$ is given by the intersection of the domain of our radical functions:

$$
[-6,\infty )\cap [-2,\infty )=[-2,\infty ),
$$

and the function is continuous on this interval.

q-105436:
Our function consists of two radical functions, so it is continuous over all points in its domain.

- To find the domain of $\sqrt{4+x}$, we set the expression under the radical to be greater than or equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}4+x\ge 0\,⟹\,x\ge -4\end{aligned}
$$

- To find the domain of $\sqrt{3x+18}$, we set the expression under the radical to be greater than or equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+18\ge 0\,⟹\,3x\ge -18\,⟹\,x\ge -6\end{aligned}
$$

The domain of $f(x)$ is given by the intersection of the domain of our radical functions:

$$
[-4,\infty )\cap [-6,\infty )=[-4,\infty ),
$$

and the function is continuous on this interval.

q-38831:
This is a rational function, so it is continuous at all points in its domain. To find its domain, we start by factoring the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x-{x}^{2}}{7x} \\  & =\frac{x(1-x)}{7x} \\  & =\frac{1-x}{7},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $x\ne 0.$

This function is continuous everywhere except at the excluded point $x=0.$

Therefore, the domain consists of the union of the intervals $(-\infty ,0),$ and $(0,\infty ),$ namely

$$
(-\infty ,0)\cup (0,\infty )
$$

and the function is also continuous on this union of intervals.

q-4561:
This is a rational function, so it is continuous at all points in its domain. To find its domain, we start by factoring the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2x+4} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2(x+2)}\end{aligned}
$$

 

This function is continuous everywhere except at the excluded point $x=-2.$

Therefore, the domain consists of the union of the intervals $(-\infty ,-2)$ and $(-2,\infty ),$ namely

$$
(-\infty ,-2)\cup (-2,\infty )
$$

and the function is also continuous on this union of intervals.

q-76071:
Our function is a logarithmic function, so it is continuous over all points in its domain.

To find the domain of ${log}_{2}⁡(\frac{2x+2}{3+{2}^{x}}),$ we set the expression under the logarithm to be greater than zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+2}{3+{2}^{x}}>0\,⟹\,2x+2>0\,⟹\,x>-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain of $f(x)={log}_{2}⁡(\frac{2x+2}{3+{2}^{x}})$ is $(-1,\infty ),$ and it is also continuous on this interval.

q-39765:
The function is a composition of two functions, a rational function, and a sine function.

The sine is continuous at all points in its domain, and its domain consists of all real numbers. So, we focus on the rational function.

Likewise, the rational function $\frac{3}{{x}^{2}-1}$ is continuous at all points in its domain. To find its domain, we start by factoring the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3}{{x}^{2}-1} \\  & =\frac{3}{(x-1)(x+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

This function is continuous everywhere except at the excluded points $x=-1$ and $x=1.$

Therefore, the domain our original function consists of the union of the intervals $(-\infty ,-1),$ $(-1,1),$ and $(1,\infty ),$ namely

$$
(-\infty ,-1)\cup (-1,1)\cup (1,\infty )
$$

and the function is also continuous on these intervals.

q-40081:
Trigonometric functions are continuous at all points in their respective domains.

The function $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ is continuous over the entire interval $[-\pi ,\pi ],$ but the function $\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ is not defined at $x=-\pi ,0,\pi .$ 

Therefore, the domain of $g(x)$ consists of the union of the intervals $(-\pi ,0)$ and $(0,\pi ),$ namely

$$
(-\pi ,0)\cup (0,\pi )
$$

and the function is also continuous on this union of intervals.
